lessons.title: Your First C++ Program
lessons.description: Program structure, standard output, the build pipeline, and the path from a source file to execution inside Nexus.
theory: Your first C++ program is not about memorizing “Hello, C++!”. It is a compact way to see several layers at once: source text, the standard library, main, standard output, the build pipeline, and execution.

C++ source code is not executed as plain text. Build tools parse and validate the program according to the language rules and prepare an executable representation. Diagnostics therefore usually belong to a specific stage of that path.

#include <iostream> makes stream I/O declarations available, std::cout names the standard output stream, and operator << inserts data into that stream. These are connected language/library concepts, not magic boilerplate.

Inside Nexus, beginner code runs in the integrated browser sandbox. You do not need to install a desktop IDE or separate compiler for the core exercises: editor, standard input, run controls, and output live in the lesson.
lessons.deep: From the beginning, separate four concepts: the C++ language, the code editor, the compiler/runtime, and the operating system. An IDE may combine several tools in one window, but it is not the language itself. Nexus Sandbox plays the educational role of an integrated environment while remaining accessible through a browser on desktop and mobile devices.
lessons.analogy: Think of a production line: the source file is the specification, preprocessing prepares the materials, the compiler validates and transforms parts, the linker assembles the product, the runtime prepares the work area, and main begins the user-written scenario.
lessons.commonMistake: Memorizing the program shape as a ritual and assuming that Visual Studio, VS Code, or another IDE “runs C++” by itself. The language, editor, build tools, and execution environment are separate layers.
lessons.task: Modify the program to print three lines: your name, “I am learning C++”, and an IT field that interests you. Use std::cout and '\n'.
lessons.hint: Use three sequential output operations. Each line can use its own std::cout statement.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the role of main in a normal C++ program?
answers: It is the special function where the user-written part of execution begins
It is the name of the standard library

terms: a general-purpose programming language; the name is read “C plus plus” and is not an acronym
the special function where the user-written part of a normal C++ program begins
a preprocessing directive that makes declarations from a header available
the standard C++ header for stream input and output
the namespace containing most of the C++ standard library
the scope-resolution operator; in std::cout it selects cout from namespace std
in this context, the stream insertion operator
the escape sequence for a newline
the build tools such as preprocessor, compiler, linker, and related components

benchmark.whyItMatters: This lesson defines the mental model used throughout the course. Instead of memorizing a Hello World template, we connect source text to the standard library, build tools, process execution, and the integrated Nexus environment. Compiler diagnostics, the sandbox, and later C++ topics then become parts of one system.
outcomes: Read a minimal C++ program and explain every construct instead of reproducing it from memory.
Distinguish the C++ language, source files, an IDE, a compiler, a linker, a runtime, and an operating system.
Explain source file → preprocessor → compiler → object code → linker → process startup → main.
Explain #include <iostream>, std::cout, ::, <<, string literals, \n, and return 0.
Classify common failures as preparation, compilation, linking, or runtime problems.
Run, modify, and validate code directly in Nexus Sandbox without requiring an external desktop IDE.
prerequisites: It is enough to know that a program is a formal sequence of instructions.
No prior experience with Visual Studio, VS Code, terminals, or compiler internals is required.
A basic everyday distinction between text and numbers is helpful; data types are taught later.
All new terminology is expanded in this lesson glossary.
quickUnderstand: C++ is the language. main.cpp is a text source file. An editor only helps you write that text.
#include <iostream> makes standard stream declarations available; it does not “insert a finished program”.
int main() defines the special main function. After startup work, normal user-written execution reaches it.
std::cout is standard output. std:: identifies the namespace and << inserts values into the stream.
"Hello, C++!\n" is a string literal; \n represents a newline.
A semicolon terminates a statement, braces delimit a block, and return 0 reports successful completion.
Nexus Sandbox combines editor, stdin, execution, and stdout in the browser, so beginner exercises do not require an external IDE.

fullTheory.lead: A minimal C++ program is tiny only in source-code size. Behind those lines are the language, standard library, preprocessing, compilation, linking, process startup, and function execution. This section follows the entire path and explains how Nexus reproduces the learning workflow inside the browser.

sections.title: 1. Language, source code, and editor are different layers
paragraphs: C++ is a programming language: rules of syntax and semantics. It is not a specific editor and not one compiler implementation.
Source code is text written according to those rules. A .cpp file is still an ordinary text file.
An editor or IDE helps create and manage that text. Visual Studio, VS Code, CLion, and Nexus are environments; none of them is the C++ language itself.

sections.title: 2. The .cpp extension and translation units
paragraphs: The .cpp extension conventionally marks C++ source files. Larger projects may contain many .cpp files plus .h or .hpp headers.
Each source file is usually processed as its own translation unit after preprocessing. The compiler analyzes that resulting unit.
This architecture allows large projects to be built in parts and later combined by the linker.

sections.title: 3. The preprocessor and #include
paragraphs: #include <iostream> is a preprocessing directive. The # at the beginning marks work that happens before the main C++ compilation phase.
A useful beginner model is that the preprocessor locates the requested header and makes its declarations visible in the translation unit.
Including a header does not run a library and does not execute code at runtime. It prepares information the compiler needs.

sections.title: 4. iostream and the standard library
paragraphs: iostream is a standard C++ header for stream I/O. I/O means Input/Output.
It provides declarations for stream objects and related operations such as std::cin, std::cout, and std::cerr.
The C++ standard library provides reusable types and facilities so programs do not need to reimplement strings, containers, streams, algorithms, and many other building blocks.

sections.title: 5. Namespaces, std, and ::
paragraphs: Large programs can contain identical short names from different components. Namespaces group names and help avoid collisions.
Most of the standard library lives in namespace std. std::cout means “cout from std”.
The double colon :: is the scope-resolution operator. Explicit qualification helps beginners see exactly where a name comes from.

sections.title: 6. main and the beginning of user code
paragraphs: A function is a named unit of executable logic. main has special status: in a normal OS-hosted program, user-written execution begins there after startup work.
int main() declares main as returning an int and taking no parameters in this form.
The operating system does not necessarily jump directly to main as the first machine instruction. Runtime startup code may execute before control reaches it.

sections.title: 7. Blocks, statements, and semicolons
paragraphs: Curly braces delimit a block. Here they define the body of main.
A statement is a complete instruction. Many C++ statements end with a semicolon, which is syntax rather than decoration.
Whitespace often does not change C++ meaning, but formatting strongly affects human readability.

sections.title: 8. std::cout and operator <<
paragraphs: std::cout is the object connected to standard output. In a terminal this usually appears as text; in Nexus it appears in the result panel.
In this context << is the stream insertion operator: std::cout << value sends a representation of value into the stream.
Insertions can be chained, for example std::cout << "x=" << x << "\n";.

sections.title: 9. String literals, escape sequences, and \n
paragraphs: Text inside double quotes is a string literal. The quote characters mark its boundaries.
Escape sequences encode special characters: \n is newline, \t is tab, and \" represents a quote inside a string.
The backslash indicates that the next character participates in a special notation, so \n is not two ordinary printed characters.

sections.title: 10. Buffering, \n, and std::endl
paragraphs: Output is often buffered so many small operations can be combined efficiently.
\n inserts a newline but does not by itself require an immediate flush. std::endl inserts a newline and also flushes the stream.
Both may look identical in a tiny example, but unnecessary flushes can be costly, so Nexus uses \n as the normal default.

sections.title: 11. return 0 and process exit status
paragraphs: return ends a function and sends a value back to its caller. In main, the returned integer becomes the process exit status.
By convention, zero indicates success while non-zero values often signal different failures.
For main specifically, reaching the closing brace without an explicit return is treated as return 0. We keep the explicit line in the first lesson for clarity.

sections.title: 12. Syntax, semantics, and diagnostics
paragraphs: Syntax asks whether code is written according to the grammar. Missing semicolons, quotes, or braces are common syntax problems.
Semantics concerns the meaning of recognized constructs: whether names exist, types match, and operations are valid.
Compiler diagnostics describe where the tool can no longer build a valid model. The real cause may be on the previous line.

sections.title: 13. Compilation, object code, and linking
paragraphs: A compiler translates a source unit into a lower-level representation and traditionally an object file.
The linker combines object files and required library definitions into the final program. A source unit can compile successfully and still fail at link time.
Distinguishing compile and link failures is essential because they require different fixes.

sections.title: 14. Runtime, process, and standard streams
paragraphs: When a program starts, the operating system creates a process with memory and other resources.
Runtime support prepares the environment used by user code. Some initialization may occur before main.
A process usually has stdin, stdout, and stderr. Nexus presents the relevant input and output streams in the lesson interface.

sections.title: 15. IDE, compiler, and Nexus Sandbox
paragraphs: IDE means Integrated Development Environment. It combines editing, navigation, running, debugging, and related tools, often by invoking a separate compiler toolchain.
VS Code is primarily an extensible editor/platform; native C++ usually requires an installed toolchain. That dependency is inconvenient for mobile-first education.
Nexus Sandbox provides an educational C++ runtime directly in the browser. Editor, stdin, run controls, output, and saved lesson state remain inside one learning environment.

sections.title: 16. Cross-platform learning and sandbox boundaries
paragraphs: Standard C++ aims for portability, but compilers, operating systems, and platform libraries can differ. Portable examples avoid unnecessary environment-specific extensions.

The current Nexus browser runtime targets educational C++ examples. It is ideal for syntax, algorithms, and core structures but is not a replacement for every capability of a production native toolchain.
As the platform grows, the same Sandbox UI can select different runtime providers while keeping the learner inside Nexus.

glossary.definition: A general-purpose programming language. The name references the ++ operator inherited from C culture; it is not a word acronym.
glossary.example: main.cpp contains C++ source code.

glossary.definition: An application that combines editor, project navigation, run/debug controls, and other development tools.
glossary.example: Visual Studio is an IDE.

glossary.definition: A text-command interface used through a terminal or shell.
glossary.example: A compiler can be invoked from a CLI.

glossary.definition: Data entering and leaving a program.
glossary.example: iostream means stream input/output facilities.

glossary.definition: Human-readable program text written in a programming language.
glossary.example: main.cpp is a source file.

glossary.definition: The stage that handles directives such as #include before core compilation.
glossary.example: #include <iostream> is handled during preprocessing.

glossary.definition: A tool that parses source code, checks language rules, and translates it to a lower-level form.
glossary.example: A syntax error is usually found during compilation.

glossary.definition: A tool that connects compiled units and library definitions into a final program.
glossary.example: A missing function definition may cause a linker error.

glossary.definition: The collection of preprocessor, compiler, linker, and related build tools.
glossary.example: GCC and Clang are parts of common C/C++ toolchains.

glossary.definition: A file or standard header containing declarations needed by other code.
glossary.example: iostream is a standard header.

glossary.definition: The result of preprocessing one source file that is analyzed by the compiler.
glossary.example: Each .cpp usually produces its own translation unit.

glossary.definition: A mechanism for grouping names and avoiding collisions.
glossary.example: cout is inside namespace std.

glossary.definition: Support state and components used while a program starts and runs.
glossary.example: Runtime initialization can happen before main.

glossary.definition: A running instance of a program managed by the operating system.
glossary.example: The same executable can be started as multiple processes.

glossary.definition: System software managing processes, memory, files, devices, and other resources.
glossary.example: Windows, Linux, Android, and iOS are operating systems.

glossary.definition: The standard input stream of a process.
glossary.example: Nexus exposes it in the input box below the editor.

glossary.definition: The main stream for normal textual program output.
glossary.example: std::cout writes to stdout.

glossary.definition: A separate stream intended for diagnostics.
glossary.example: Native applications can redirect stderr separately from stdout.

glossary.definition: An integer reporting how a process finished.
glossary.example: return 0 from main conventionally signals success.

glossary.definition: Forcing buffered output to be forwarded immediately.
glossary.example: std::endl inserts a newline and performs a flush.

inside.title: 1. Source file
inside.text: You edit main.cpp, an ordinary text file containing C++ source code.

inside.title: 2. Preprocessor
inside.text: #include and other directives are handled to form the translation unit.

inside.title: 3. Compiler
inside.text: Syntax, names, and types are analyzed and an internal/lower-level representation is generated.

inside.title: 4. Object code
inside.text: A compiled unit becomes object code plus metadata needed for final assembly.

inside.title: 5. Linker
inside.text: Object modules and required library definitions are connected into the final program.

inside.title: 6. Loader / Runtime
inside.text: The system creates a process, loads the program, and prepares runtime state and standard streams.

inside.title: 7. main
inside.text: Control reaches main, where the user-written scenario begins.

inside.title: 8. Exit status
inside.text: The value returned from main becomes the process exit status; zero conventionally means success.

walkthrough.explanation: A preprocessing directive that makes standard stream I/O declarations available.
A blank line is only for humans: it visually separates includes from the function definition.
Define the special main function returning int and open its body.
Select cout from std, insert a string literal into the output stream, and append a newline.
Finish main and report successful process completion with exit status 0.
Close the block that forms the body of main.

experiments.title: Remove #include <iostream>
experiments.change: Delete the first line and run the code in Nexus Sandbox.
experiments.predict: Decide whether the problem occurs before execution or during execution.
experiments.explanation: The compiler no longer sees the required standard-output declarations, so main never starts.

experiments.title: Remove std::
experiments.change: Keep cout but do not add using namespace std.
experiments.predict: Which part of the full name is missing?
experiments.explanation: cout is inside namespace std; std:: qualifies the name.

experiments.title: Remove the semicolon
experiments.predict: Which line might the diagnostic point to?
experiments.explanation: The parser may only prove the previous construct is incomplete when it reads the next token.

experiments.title: Replace \n with std::endl
experiments.explanation: The newline usually looks the same, but std::endl also flushes the stream.

experiments.title: Remove return 0
experiments.change: Close main immediately after the output statement.
experiments.predict: Will a valid program still compile?
experiments.explanation: Yes. Reaching the end of main is treated as returning zero.

experiments.title: Add another output
experiments.change: Print another line and an integer such as 2026.
experiments.predict: Do you need another header just to print an int?
experiments.explanation: std::cout already supports many fundamental types; a separate header is not needed for a basic int.

errors.title: cout is not declared
errors.symptom: The environment reports that cout cannot be found.
errors.reason: The code uses cout as a global name although it lives in namespace std.

errors.title: Missing semicolon
errors.symptom: The diagnostic may point at return or the next line.
errors.reason: The output statement is not terminated.

errors.title: Typographic quotes
errors.symptom: Unexpected characters or invalid tokens are reported.
errors.reason: Smart quotes are not C++ string delimiters.

errors.title: main has no return type
errors.symptom: A modern compiler rejects the function definition.
errors.reason: C++ requires an explicit function return type.

errors.title: Unterminated string literal
errors.symptom: The compiler reports an unterminated string or unexpected tokens.
errors.reason: The opening double quote has no matching closing quote.
errors.fix: Close the string literal before the semicolon.

errors.title: Debugging the wrong stage
errors.wrongCode: // The program builds but prints the wrong text
errors.symptom: The learner keeps changing syntax although compilation already succeeds.
errors.reason: A compile error and a logical error are different categories.
errors.fix: First determine whether code fails to build, fails to start, or starts and produces the wrong result.

practice.title: Three lines
practice.prompt: Print your name, “I am learning C++”, and your chosen IT field.

practice.title: Classify the failure
practice.prompt: Remove #include, std::, and ; one at a time. For each case write stage, symptom, cause, and fix.
practice.hint: All three prevent successful execution, but for different reasons.

practice.title: IDE or compiler?
practice.prompt: Explain the difference between the C++ language, an editor/IDE, and a compiler. Give one example of each.
practice.hint: C++ defines rules; an IDE helps you work; a compiler validates/translates source code.

practice.title: Mini profile
practice.prompt: Build a small text profile in Nexus Sandbox: heading, name, field, learning goal, and a separator. Design the expected output before coding.
practice.hint: Start from the desired screen output, then write the program.

lab.title: Lab: the lifecycle of your first program
lab.goal: Demonstrate understanding of the stages that connect source code to execution, not merely produce Hello World.
steps: Use “Test runtime” in Nexus Sandbox and confirm that the embedded environment can execute a control program.
Run the reference example and record stdout.
Change the string literal and confirm that only user-visible output changes.
Create one syntax error, read the diagnostic, and explain why main never starts.
Remove std:: from cout and explain the namespace failure.
Remove return 0 and observe valid program behavior.
Without hints, explain source → preprocess → compile → link → runtime → main → exit code.
lab.proof: The lab is complete when the learner can run code inside Nexus without an external IDE, explain every line, and classify a typical failure stage.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which item is a programming language rather than a development environment?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: C++ defines the language rules. Visual Studio is an IDE and VS Code is an extensible editor/platform.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why does std::cout require <iostream> declarations?
answers: iostream makes the stream I/O declarations available
main does not exist without iostream
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The header provides declarations for standard stream interfaces.

knowledgeCheck.question: Compilation succeeds but a required function definition cannot be connected. Which stage fails?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The linker connects definitions from compiled units and libraries.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is \n often preferred to std::endl for ordinary output?
answers: \n does not require an extra flush
knowledgeCheck.explanation: std::endl inserts a newline and also flushes the stream; that extra operation is not always needed.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does Nexus Sandbox provide in this lesson?
answers: It requires VS Code to be installed
Integrated editor, stdin, execution, and stdout in the browser
It only displays code without running it
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The core learning loop stays inside the platform.

sandboxModel.title: Nexus Sandbox — integrated practice environment
sandboxModel.description: Editor, standard input, execution, and output stay inside the lesson. Beginner exercises do not require moving source code to VS Code or another IDE.
points: Code is saved with lesson progress.
stdin and stdout are next to the editor.
Execution uses a browser-based educational runtime; no local C++ toolchain is required for this lesson.
A self-test button verifies runtime availability before an exercise.
The learning flow is designed for keyboard and touch interaction instead of depending on a desktop IDE.
sandboxModel.limit: The current browser runtime targets an educational subset of C++. Later the same Nexus Sandbox interface can route advanced lessons to a local engine or secure compiler backend when a full native toolchain is required.

summary: I can distinguish C++, a source file, an IDE, a compiler, a linker, and a runtime.
I can explain every line of a minimal C++ program.
I understand #include, iostream, std::, std::cout, <<, \n, ;, and return 0.
I can describe the path from main.cpp to a running process.
I can distinguish compilation, linking, and runtime problems.
I can complete a basic C++ exercise directly in Nexus Sandbox without switching to external software.
modernNotes: Nexus uses explicit std::cout rather than a global using namespace std; in the reference example.
Ordinary line breaks use \n; std::endl is reserved for cases that really need a flush.
The example is independent of IDE-specific precompiled-header mechanisms.
Practice remains inside Nexus Sandbox; a desktop IDE is optional rather than mandatory.
historicalContext: Older environment-specific examples can still matter when reading legacy code, but they are not presented as the modern portable baseline.
Source provenance is maintained in internal project documentation instead of being mixed into the learner-facing lesson.
